rendered:
The review does not recommend tens of nanometres for low-diffusivity oxides such as ZrO2. Its recommendation is the opposite: coating thickness should stay thin. The review says that the most widely used cost-effective coating materials have very low lithium-ion diffusivity, and that their maximum thickness is usually recommended to be around ∼10 nm[1] for effective use of the coating benefits. Its calculations also say the ideal thickness should be below ten nanometers[2] for better electrochemical performance. The "tens of nanometres" figure appears only as a description of the literature: tens of nanometers[3] is the typical reported thickness, because thickness is difficult to control with easily scalable processes.

The reasoning given is as follows. The review states that the lithium-ion diffusivity of most oxides and fluorides is is extremely low, particularly for ZrO2[4]. It estimated diffusion time with a simple relation based on diffusion length and diffusivity, varying the diffusion length from from 5nm to 50nm[5]. The result was that longer diffusion times are observed for thicker coating layers[6]. Because the measured electrochemical performance is limited by ionic diffusion through the coating, a thicker low-diffusivity layer slows lithium transport and hurts performance, so thin layers are favoured.

A second reason is chemical. Inert, stable oxides such as ZrO2 or Al2O3 may react with lithium ions and form secondary phases[7] (for ZrO2, for example Li2ZrO3), resulting in capacity fading issue[8]. Keeping the layer thin limits this loss of capacity.

The review also notes that thicker coatings of some materials still give good rate capability, which it says is not clearly explained in the literature. It proposes that lithium-containing compositions may form in the low-diffusivity oxides during cycling, which would raise ionic diffusivity in the coating. This is offered as an expectation, not as a reason to use tens of nanometres.
